Workers should follow their boss's lead when it comes to talking business in the gym.

Jacob Wackerhausen/Getty Images

  • Working out with your boss may be awkward, but it's becoming the norm at some companies.
  • Fitness coaches, etiquette experts, and execs shared tips to make the experience feel less awkward.
  • Some said that workers should come prepared to the workout, but shouldn't try to outdo their boss.

Zach Schofel, cofounder and CEO of lease platform Cosign, gives new employees two options: a 7:20 a.m. Barry's class or a padel session.

"It's good to do something to meet and hang out with someone, get to know someone before you start," Schofel told Business Insider.

Welcome to the modern workplace, where post-work drinks are out and HIIT classes with your boss are the new norm. As companies embrace health and wellness — and look for alternatives to happy hours as drinking rates decline — coworkers are turning to workouts to bond, and, ideally, impress their managers.

Longevity fitness is one of the hottest trends right now among high-performers in business, tech, and finance. Being able to speak the language on key concepts like VO2 max, grip strength, and resistance training can earn you serious credibility if your supervisor is a gym rat, said CEO Maria Colacurcio, who runs software company Syndio.

"You're going to get more respect, and you're going to immediately open a rapport and a relationship at a level that wasn't open to you before," said Colacurio, who competes as a pro-level Hyrox athlete and works out with employees and board members.

If you haven't been invited to a team workout yet, it may only be a matter of time. Business Insider spoke with fitness instructors, CEOs, job coaches, etiquette experts, and employees who work out together about the dos and don'ts of sweating it out with your boss.

Look up the workout beforehand — and know your limits

A networking workout can quickly backfire if you've overstated your qualifications or can't bring real enthusiasm to the effort.

To make the most of a workout with your manager in the room, you should have some basic fitness knowledge and competency. Plus, if your boss asks you to spot them, you want to know what you're doing.

"I would want to make sure that I know every single workout that we're going to do," Noah Neiman, cofounder of group fitness studio The Pack, told Business Insider.

Stay self-aware about your strengths and weaknesses. There's no point picking up a 30lb over a 25lb.

"Nine times out of 10, nobody's clocking that — that's our own ego and insecurity getting in the way," Nic Wilson, an F45 athlete, said.

Even lifting an empty barbell can make a good impression if you're making a genuine effort to improve, according to Colacurio. "Being confident and knowledgeable about your journey, I would see that and be so impressed," she said.

Colacurcio said she frequently works out with board members before a meeting. From left: Byron Deeter and Talia Goldberg (from Bessemer Venture Partners), Colacurcio, and her husband, Brandon Hughes.

Courtesy of Maria Colacurcio

Still, you should be prepared to get a little uncomfortable — scaling a workout to fit your needs is OK, but complaining or changing it excessively can be disruptive.

If you're unfamiliar with the workout style, try a class on your own first. You'll know what to expect, get a feel for the format, and avoid looking lost in front of the person signing off on your next performance review.

Don't try to outdo them

Neiman regularly hosts corporate workouts at his gym. His tip to employees? Give it your all and don't complain about how difficult the workout is — but don't try to one-up your boss. In fact, trying too hard could have the opposite effect.

"I hate a suck-up," Neiman, who has trained executives, said.

Noah Neiman is the cofounder of group fitness studio The Pack.

Noah Neiman

The better strategy is to read the room.

"Try to map your effort to the human that you're meeting. If they're really intense, you can be really intense," said Colacurio, who works out with members of her board and potential investors as well as employees.

Especially in a one-on-one situation, matching their pace, even at a lower intensity, can build more rapport than blowing past your workout buddy.

It's a delicate balance. In a group setting, pushing yourself can highlight your drive and work ethic, as long as the competition stays friendly.

"I also want my investors to see that I'm competitive," said Colacurio. "I leave it all on the field."

Wait to talk shop

Some employees told Business Insider they use workout classes as a chance to get extra one-on-one time with their boss and to ask questions they don't always have time to address in the office. For others, business conversations are off-limits once they're in the studio. The gym is for working out, not discussing the latest deal or unanswered emails.

It all depends on your relationship with your manager and their perspective on it — so the safest approach is to let them set the tone.

Gottsman said workers should let their boss take the lead in bringing up work conversations.

"Don't bring up business, don't bring up closing a deal," Gottsman said. "Unless they do it first."

Colacurio said the biggest mistake employees make is to talk shop too early or too often.

"The beauty of working out together is it's kind of like the business dinner where it's relational, not transactional," she said. "The best business dinners, you don't get to the business until the very end."

Wear tonal colors

Diane Gottsman, who owns The Protocol School of Texas, which specializes in professional development and corporate etiquette training, recommends avoiding flashy clothing and dressing as though you could run into your best client at the gym.

Victoria Repa, CEO and founder of BetterMe, an all-in-one well-being platform, said a tonal look in black, chocolate, navy, or ivory is a safe bet and can give you an "effortlessly polished" look.

"The only real 'don't' is anything you'll spend the entire class adjusting, or anything you choose solely to impress the room," Repa said.

If you don't want to work out, suggest another activity

However, if you're not comfortable working out with your boss or feel overly anxious about it, don't force it.

The goal is to build a stronger relationship with your manager or coworkers, Ron Porter, a senior client partner at Korn Ferry, told Business Insider.

If your boss invites you to play golf and you've never picked up a club, it may be better to suggest another activity, such as tennis or a walk.

Even if your boss loves working out, that's unlikely to be your only chance to spend time together outside the office. Schofel said he organizes workouts with his team because he enjoys them and sees them as a way to connect with employees. However, he isn't keeping track of who doesn't show up.

items.title: We moved our 3 aging parents into 2 tiny homes in our yard for $100k. It made caregiving possible.
items.summary: Linda Barton's parents have adjusted to life in their tiny home. Linda Barton Linda Barton and her husband moved their parents into tiny homes to manage their elder care. Balancing full-time jobs with long-term care, Barton navigates financial and healthcare challenges. Linda faces choosing between funding her retirement and paying for caregivers for her older parents. This as-told-to interview is based on a conversation with Linda Barton, 55, who lives in Texas with her husband and works in criminal justice for the courts. They moved their three living parents into tiny homes in their yard to afford their care and manage their full-time work schedules. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. I was clueless and in my 40s when this journey began. I think most people are like me. I'm always throwing out ideas to people to help them navigate these years of their lives. My parents were older when they had me, and I'm 18 and 16 years younger than my older brothers, both of whom died by the time I was 20. My dad died when I was 30, and they were married for 52 years. My mom worked in accounting, and my dad was a truck driver and construction worker . Are you paying for your own or your loved one's long-term care? Have you considered alternative housing options for your family? To share your story with a reporter, please fill out this quick form . Eight years after he died, my mom remarried. That was about 17 years ago; she was 75, and he was 73. She was very active in her 60s and 70s, working at a local state prison as a grievance clerk and a corrections officer. My stepfather had been in recovery from a massive stroke when they met, but they were both active into their 80s. At 85, my mom started to have AFib problems. She already had a heart stent. She got a pacemaker, and things went downhill from there. She had a collapsed lung as well. They realized they couldn't take care of themselves anymore. They wanted to stay at their home, but they lived 17 miles in the opposite direction from my job, which is an hour away. It was wearing me out going back and forth to check on them. I work in criminal justice for the courts. My husband is a superintendent in the commercial HVAC industry, managing multiple job sites. And he doesn't have a set schedule. We started talking about tiny homes. I didn't fully understand how much it would cost to do the whole setup. We were seeing some as high as $130,000. My parents had Social Security and small retirements, but they didn't have the money to pay that sort of mortgage. Linda Barton and her husband purchased two tiny homes for their parents. Linda Barton We found a place that does portable buildings that are already converted to tiny homes inside, and they were within what they could afford for their monthly payments. We own a house on eight acres, so we have the space. My husband is handy and was able to set up a lot of their utilities himself, including laying the water lines, installing the electricity, and building the driveway. Getting the permit and installing a new electrical line costs around $2,000. We got a heavy discount on installing a septic system because we have a friend who does that professionally. We suspect the setup would've cost upward of $20,000 if we hadn't done a lot of it ourselves, which halved the price. My parents put a $5,000 down payment on the house, which we bought for $37,000. They pay a little over $600 a month. We did install a ramp on their home, which wasn't too expensive. A year later, we got another tiny house for my father-in-law. Shortly before, my father-in-law started having health issues. We found him on the floor a few times, and he was 40 miles away. We went back to the same place and bought another home for $43,000, and we paid the down payment. We're glad we moved the three of them in when we did because they're not able to live alone anymore. My mom has dementia and is in hospice, but for a while, my parents and father-in-law had higher functioning. The two tiny homes are right next to each other. Linda Barton Navigating their healthcare has been a nightmare. My mom still knows my stepdad and me and others around her, but she's not capable of doing anything more than what you would expect of a child. My stepfather acts like he's 6 years old. He can turn on the TV and tell you what he wants, but he doesn't make meals or do other errands. My father-in-law is like a 13-year-old who wants to live life and do all the fun stuff, but he doesn't want to do anything that comes with it, like doing laundry or taking care of his vehicle. We started out with one caregiver through the VA, because my stepfather is a veteran, but did not serve during wartime and is only 10% disabled. His benefits are therefore more limited, and the maximum caregiver assistance that he can get is 20 hours a week. My mom gets no benefits through the VA. Eventually, we added another caregiver in the evening. As my mom got progressively worse, we hired somebody to come in the mornings to get her going. Medicare does not pay for care providers, which a lot of people don't realize. Medicaid will pay for people to come in, but my parents don't get Medicaid, at least not yet. I've been researching getting Medicaid to come help pay for a caregiver, but there is a two to three-year waiting list. I wish I had known that earlier. We also now pay for a third caregiver for my father-in-law, coming two or three days a week, to help clean his house and do simple tasks. The tiny homes have enough space for their parents. Linda Barton We're hanging in there as long as we can. These are our parents, and we do what needs to be done to take care of them. Still, there's absolutely no regard in the medical system for the fact that we have jobs. I'll get 15 calls in a day, and thankfully, I work a job where I can sometimes stop and answer them most of the time. A lot of people can't. Then, you can never reach them when you call back. It's like phone tag. Linda Barton provides as much care as she can for her parents. Linda Barton My husband and I have a decent income. We live in a rural area, and we're blessed because our income is good and probably higher than the average out here. I have a pension from my job, which I can get starting in two years, and he has a 401(k), but we both waited too long to start planning for a situation like this. We're at a crossroads where we have to choose between putting money into my retirement or paying for my parents' caregivers. If we don't pay for caregivers, we end up sacrificing work when they need something. It's a constant balancing act for us between our finances, helping them, and making sure we still have money when we're older. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: On Wall Street, barely sleeping was a badge of honor. It inspired me to quit and launch a health startup.
items.summary: Josh Hou, on the right, with his Ren cofounders Ryan Hou (left) and Eli Qian (middle). Josh Hou Josh Hou, 22, left his investment banking job at Evercore after a year to cofound Ren, a health app. Conversations on Wall Street about sleep and the culture around wearables inspired the startup. Hou quit three months before getting his bonus, hoping to minimize his regret later. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Josh Hou, 22, who left his job as an investment banking analyst at Evercore to co-found Ren, an app that helps users determine how specific interventions, like specific supplements, are affecting their health by running experiments on the body. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. As an investment banking analyst at Evercore, sleep was by far the most common subject of conversation. Not sleeping was almost like a badge of honor. It proved you were working on the coolest deals. Some of us relied on caffeine, others on nicotine, which made it harder to stay healthy overall. A few months ago, my best friend and I began talking about founding a health optimization company together, and I realized that analysts should focus on making the most of the few hours of rest they get. Lots of my coworkers used Whoops, or Apple Watches , or Oura Rings, but it seemed like most people just accepted their health was going to be messed up for the next two years. Hou, left, has known one of his cofounders since they were children. Josh Hou We eventually came up with Ren, partly because I realized that people often didn't measure the outcomes of healthcare choices. They'd take a peptide or supplement without ever keeping track of the results. I couldn't focus on the company while working banking hours — my cofounder and I would email during the day since I didn't want to be on my phone — so I decided to quit three months before my bonus, after about a year at Evercore. It might seem weird that I didn't stick it out until my bonus, but I live by Jeff Bezos' regret minimization framework. A decade from now, I assume I'd regret staying in banking more than missing out on the roughly $50,000 bonus I might have made. Hopefully, that money won't be a huge deal to me by that point. Banking was never my calling I started on the finance track as a freshman at UT Austin. It sometimes felt like there were only two career options for the smartest, most successful kids: banking and consulting. Within the first few weeks on campus, I was bombarded with invitations to different club info sessions and coffee chats, and eventually was one of the few people to get into my investment team. Some of my friends truly loved finance. They'd read finance books and watch finance movies, but I always found myself on Twitter and online reading about the tech world. But I knew I'd feel left out if I didn't go through banking recruiting , and by sophomore year, I landed a summer internship at Evercore. The tech world wasn't my only outside interest — I've been into fitness since I was a little kid. Growing up, I played pretty much every sport, but I was still chubby. I'd eat two lunches most days, one that my mom packed and one from the church across the street from school, and go to McDonald's for a snack before swim practice. When COVID hit my junior year of high school, I had nothing to focus on but losing weight. By senior year, I was in the best shape of my life. My mom told me not to take protein powder or creatine , and instead pushed the health hacks she read about from Chinese influencers online. That's when I first started wondering how you can verify what actually works for your body. Hou has completed marathons and Ironmans. Josh Hou College meant an unlimited meal plan, more drinking, and a longer walk to the gym, and I gained 30 pounds my freshman year. I constantly battled my weight, losing it all, gaining it back, losing it again, gaining it again. People say you can't outwork a bad diet, but I sure as hell tried between marathons, Ironmans, and gym sessions. My Instagram feed was full of these super jacked guys, which made the insecurity and body dysmorphia that much worse. The cycle continued during my 10-week banking internship. I was just too tired, stressed, or worried about other things to get to the gym . When I got back to school, I locked in, trained for an Ironman, and lost the pounds I gained, and health was top of mind when I returned to Evercore full-time. I was preparing to leave for a few months Between the lifestyle and my interest in the tech world, I knew early on in my job that I might leave banking to do something risky. At the beginning of this year, I stopped contributing to my retirement account, and I've now liquidated my savings from my year in banking. I know I can always move home if I really need to. There were so many more practical reasons to stay in finance than to leave, especially since we had the app's basics but no users by the time I left. AI is making it easier than ever to found a company , and our initial platform was entirely vibe-coded. My parents weren't initially thrilled I was leaving my safe finance job , but they've eventually come around. I told them the morning I decided to quit, and their support was the last bit of confidence I needed to tell my manager and the rest of my team members, who weren't too surprised. We have around 40 beta users, mostly friends who care about their health. A lot of my day is spent iterating on their feedback — fixing bugs, going over requests for new features, all that stuff — or thoughts we got from people at our gym. I also spend a lot of time preparing for launch and thinking about how to attract investors, along with training for a marathon with one of my cofounders. Now, I have time for both sleep and a workout. Eventually, we want to sell every component of health experiments through Ren, like supplements and blood tests, but for now, we're focused on getting on the app store. I'd eat two lunches most days, one that my mom packed and one from the church across the street from school, and go to McDonald's for a snack before swim practice.

When COVID hit my junior year of high school, I had nothing to focus on but losing weight. By senior year, I was in the best shape of my life. My mom told me not to take protein powder or creatine, and instead pushed the health hacks she read about from Chinese influencers online. That's when I first started wondering how you can verify what actually works for your body.

Hou has completed marathons and Ironmans.

Josh Hou

College meant an unlimited meal plan, more drinking, and a longer walk to the gym, and I gained 30 pounds my freshman year. I constantly battled my weight, losing it all, gaining it back, losing it again, gaining it again. People say you can't outwork a bad diet, but I sure as hell tried between marathons, Ironmans, and gym sessions. My Instagram feed was full of these super jacked guys, which made the insecurity and body dysmorphia that much worse.

The cycle continued during my 10-week banking internship. I was just too tired, stressed, or worried about other things to get to the gym. When I got back to school, I locked in, trained for an Ironman, and lost the pounds I gained, and health was top of mind when I returned to Evercore full-time.

I was preparing to leave for a few months

Between the lifestyle and my interest in the tech world, I knew early on in my job that I might leave banking to do something risky. At the beginning of this year, I stopped contributing to my retirement account, and I've now liquidated my savings from my year in banking. I know I can always move home if I really need to.

There were so many more practical reasons to stay in finance than to leave, especially since we had the app's basics but no users by the time I left. AI is making it easier than ever to found a company, and our initial platform was entirely vibe-coded.

My parents weren't initially thrilled I was leaving my safe finance job, but they've eventually come around. I told them the morning I decided to quit, and their support was the last bit of confidence I needed to tell my manager and the rest of my team members, who weren't too surprised.

We have around 40 beta users, mostly friends who care about their health. A lot of my day is spent iterating on their feedback — fixing bugs, going over requests for new features, all that stuff — or thoughts we got from people at our gym. I also spend a lot of time preparing for launch and thinking about how to attract investors, along with training for a marathon with one of my cofounders. Now, I have time for both sleep and a workout.

Eventually, we want to sell every component of health experiments through Ren, like supplements and blood tests, but for now, we're focused on getting on the app store.

items.title: Gen Z's new anti-tech rebellion: making eye contact and listening to each other
items.summary: Members of the Luddite Club gather in New York City's Tomkins Square Park. Corrie Aune for BI Members of New York City's Luddite Club yearn for a life without a screen. Some have given up smartphones. Others have more radical ideas. They say limiting technology has made their lives richer and allowed them to connect with others. Jameson Butler hated how much time she spent on her smartphone , so over the pandemic, she ditched it for a flip phone. It was meant to be a temporary "social media cleanse." Years later, the 19-year-old still hasn't gone back. "Immediately, the quality of my life increased so dramatically," she said during a meetup of like-minded tech skeptics in New York City's Tompkins Square Park on Sunday. "I was like, oh my God, we've all been sold this lie that we have to have phones." Butler cofounded the Luddite Club in 2021, a group whose members meet weekly in the city to discuss literature, life, and the pitfalls of technology. For its members, each meeting is a rare couple of hours where they can experience social connection that isn't set up by an Instagram DM or a text blast. Members of the Luddite Club hang out in the park without a phone in sight. Corrie Aune for BI In some meetings, the group goes on walks or does scavenger hunts around the city. In others, they smash iPads into the concrete and wear pointy paper hats. In every meeting, the group hopes to show people that life offline is fulfilling, organic, and fun. "We found the phone and the social media and the constant communication technology so invasive to our lives," said cofounder Logan Lane, a 21-year-old student at Oberlin College. There were about 20 Luddites who showed up at the park. They sat in the grass and talked about literature and their apartments, a time-honored conversation topic in New York City. One played an accordion. The raucous din of a nearby street hockey game occasionally interrupted conversations about "Animal Farm" and other classics. It was Eddie Friedland's first meeting. A 22-year-old art teacher, he said he decided to join because he felt he was spending too much time on Instagram Reels. Eddie Friedland said he watches too many Instagram Reels. Corrie Aune for BI "I'm thinking about giving up on the phone," Friedland said. "I'm up all night on Reels." Barrett Shepard, a 20-year-old Brooklyn resident and longtime Luddite, listened as Friedland laid out his problem. "You just coming here and finding out about this makes that almost a shifting in the way you're thinking," Shepard told him. "That's what I think is really cool." The club, which takes its name from the mythical leader of a group of British artisans who protested the Industrial Revolution in the 1800s by destroying textile machinery, has grown in prominence at a time when Gen Z is responding with growing scorn to artificial intelligence and social media, innovations they say cheapen their lives and detract from human-to-human connection. Barrett Shepard is a longtime member of the Luddite Club. Corrie Aune for BI In a Gallup poll released in April, 31% of Gen Z respondents (those born between 1997 and 2012) reported feeling "anger" toward AI, up from 22% a year before. In a Pew Research study released Tuesday, 55% of Americans under 30 reported feeling more concerned than excited about AI. Anti-tech reactionaries have put garbage bags over AI-powered Flock cameras, which read license plates to aid law enforcement. Some have shot them with guns. Online content creators who advertise or use AI are facing backlash from their audiences. And Americans are rallying across the country to protest AI data centers . The members of the Luddite club differ in how they put their anti-tech values into practice. Not everyone has a flip phone, for example, and Lane said the group isn't dogmatically against technology. "Historical Luddites are constantly misinterpreted as totally anti-technology, and we're not totally anti-technology," she said. "We're anti-technology that is not helpful to our lives." Lane, Butler, and a few others comprise a group of more hardcore Luddite members who have done away with smartphones altogether. Some members of this group prefer a model of flip phone with no app store and only the barest abilities. A flip phone used by a Luddite. Corrie Aune for BI "Just call, text, photos, and there's a notes app," Butler said. Some, like Ryan Bailey, have more radical concerns about a future surveillance state powered by artificial intelligence. "I've hated modern technology for a long time," the 40-year-old Manhattan resident said. "More people are catching onto that now." Not everyone at the gathering said they were ready to give up their smartphones . Miquel Enrigue, a 30-year-old freelance filmmaker who lives in Brooklyn, said social media is the only reliable way for him to find gigs. "What I would really like is to be able to survive without it," he said of platforms like Instagram. "But it's just increasingly more difficult." Even Bailey said he keeps an Instagram page to find events and shows in the city. Lane said that being part of the club involves "constant experimenting" to find what level of tech works best for each member. Shepard uses a flip phone when possible, but also uses a laptop at college to complete assignments. A Luddite plays an accordion. Corrie Aune for BI "I don't think Luddism is having a flip phone," Shepard said. "The flip phone is a cool thing to pull out, but it doesn't change any habits." Shepard uses the phone solely to organize meetings with friends. Shepard recalled, with admiration, the stories passed down by parents about their teenage years, when they met friends by chance on the street. "You live in a city with public space and places to meet," Shepard said. "You don't need technology." Mayla Burnstein, a 20-year-old Kindergarten teacher in Manhattan, said the Luddite meetings help people "relearn" basic skills they lost growing up with their noses in screens, like how to look others in the eye and be fully present in a conversation. "Big tech has made us feel very inward-facing, and that becomes very self-isolating," she said. "Those moments where we manage to turn outward, and to observe, engage, and interact - that's where that shows up." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: I spent decades pleasing everyone. Then cancer changed the equation.
items.summary: The author, pictured with her husband, said she has been a lifelong people pleaser. A cancer diagnosis gave her a crash course in setting boundaries. Courtesy of Lynn Shattuck. As a firstborn Gen-X daughter, people-pleasing was like a second skin to me. Discovering I had chronic lymphoma forced me to set boundaries and maintain boundaries. I've found that setting boundaries gets easier with practice, but requires vigilance. The summer I turned 50, I was diagnosed with lymphoma . While the type I have is considered to be very treatable, it's also considered chronic. "You'll likely die with it, not of it," my oncologist told me. The one-two punch of turning 50 and receiving a cancer diagnosis became a crash course on managing another chronic ailment that's long plagued me, people pleasing . As a firstborn daughter , disappointing people I love has always felt physically painful to me. When my son was a toddler, and I'd leave to go to a yoga class, he'd sob as we watched me through the window, his face scrunched up like he was being tortured. I'd try to override the ache in my chest as I backed the car out of the driveway, reminding myself that my son was safe in my husband's care, and it was healthy for me to take a little time to nurture myself. As my kids grew and I attended regular therapy, the silent, impossible expectations of myself that I hadn't realized I'd been carrying started to appear, like invisible ink being revealed. I started to see that the flood of guilt I felt when I put my kids in part-time childcare or hesitated to volunteer at their schools was neither necessary nor healthy. Cancer offered clarity Lymphoma occurs when the white blood cells responsible for fighting infections mutate and multiply. People-pleasing, I've learned through the years, is, for women, a cultural norm and often a survival tactic . It's meant to keep us safe, but if unchecked, it gnaws at us, depleting us. Cancer brought my people-pleasing into sharper contrast. When someone asked me to do something I didn't have the time, energy, or desire to do, I began to feel a "no" rising up. I'd start to push it away, as I'd always done. But a quiet voice said, "You have cancer. You can say no." Sometimes my nos were silent, like deleting the school emails looking for parent volunteers. Other times, they were more challenging, like when my mom asked for a ride home from the ER late one night when she was sick. To battle the tug of guilt, I summoned that quiet, wise voice, and I heard, "You need to rest. Mom can get an Uber." Sometimes the boundaries were just for me, like deciding to swap out our oversized SUV for a smaller car because I was tired of the anxiety that flooded me every time I pulled into our garage. Practice makes it easier With practice, it became easier to set boundaries . Boundaries, I began to see, are actually benevolent, because they communicate our needs and limits to others. I began speaking up about things I wouldn't have in the past. No, I really don't want Chinese food tonight, I'd say, gritting my teeth for a moment before realizing I could exhale. I'd stated a preference, a need, or a limit — and the world had kept on spinning. As women, the world will give us as much as we can carry, and then it will pile a few more blocks of concrete on for good measure. We're the only ones who can say, "That's enough." I'm now two years out from my initial diagnosis, and I still see my oncologist once a quarter. As the doctors look over my bloodwork, I check in with myself. Am I still setting boundaries when they're called for? Is my work-life in balance? Am I prioritizing my well-being and scheduling things to look forward to? Like lymphoma, people-pleasing requires surveillance. It's a chronic condition, and one I'll be working on for the long haul. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: I’m Eva Longoria. I'm a media-company cofounder with a militant sleep routine, but I make time for my son and a glass of wine.
items.summary: Eva Longoria. Courtesy of Eva Longoria This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Eva Longoria, a 51-year-old actor, producer, director, and entrepreneur who lives between Spain, Mexico, and the US. It has been edited for length and clarity. I'm an actor who started in my early 20s. I never imagined it as a career growing up, but after entering a talent contest, I decided to move to LA and give acting a real shot. My first professional acting jobs were on television. One of my first major TV roles was on "The Young and the Restless." My breakout role came soon after, as Gabrielle Solis on " Desperate Housewives ." Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful leaders in business structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine. At this point in my career, I'm focused on Hyphenate Media Group , a next-generation media company I cofounded that develops, produces, and invests in culture-defining premium film, television, and digital content. Here's a day in my life. I wake up around 5 a.m. with my son, Santi He's basically my alarm clock. I get up, get dressed, and the first thing I do is make him fresh tortillas every morning. Then I drink a glass of water before heading to my workout. I usually work out around 5:30 a.m. During my hourlong workout, I like to mix it up with heavy strength training and functional movement. I love to bounce and walk. I change my routine pretty often, but consistency is what really matters. It's less about doing the perfect workout and more about showing up every day. I use amino acids and supplements for training. After that, I have the same breakfast every morning: boiled eggs — no yolk — and turkey sausage. I eat breakfast in the car with Santi While I drive him to school, I also drink my water with electrolytes and creatine. I wear a lot of different hats. My days vary depending on what I'm doing because I'm an entrepreneur at heart, so I'm constantly working on different projects. I head to the office by 9 a.m. After dropping Santi off, I'll head to the office. It takes me about an hour. If I have meetings — which I often do — I'll be driven so I can work in the car. Sometimes I take Waymo rides to make it easier. In the car, I do Zooms, take calls, and answer emails. I also have a lot of Zooms in the morning because I do a lot of work in Europe, and the time difference is hard when I'm in LA. I try to stack everything early and be very efficient so that once I'm home, I can actually be present. I take a lot of meetings When I'm in the office, I'm jumping between meetings about rewrites or reviewing scripts that come in for film development. Every meeting is different. When the team is all together in the same room, we brainstorm. Sometimes our meetings are development meetings, writer meetings, or pitches. We're in the middle of a lot of pitches right now. We also have branding meetings constantly — I think we had eight brands come through recently for branded content we're producing. We have our unscripted side and our scripted side, so I'm meeting with our unscripted executives to go over the slate — who we're selling to, what stage it's at, whether it's sold, pitching, in production, or in post. When I'm directing, I sometimes shoot 12-hour days When I'm directing, it feels like full steam ahead. Call time is often 6 a.m., so on those days, I wake up around 4 a.m. to work out at 4:30 a.m. and leave the house by 5:30 a.m. We usually have 12-hour shoots. I don't like running sets that are longer than 12 hours. On "Desperate Housewives," we would sometimes shoot for 17 or 18 hours. The 18-hour days are gone. People need to go home to their families. You have to have a civilized life. When I shoot in places like Spain or France, there are rules that you can't go above certain hours, and I love that. When we're shooting, I sometimes stop and realize I haven't eaten all day. My assistant literally has to keep me fed and make sure I'm drinking water. I go through two big bottles of water a day when I'm on set. Things always feel a bit crazy when I'm directing. Soccer teams, investments, and building businesses I also spend time on my other projects — my soccer teams, investments, and entrepreneurial work. I'm an investor in several soccer clubs, including Angel City FC, Club Necaxa, and La Equidad in Bogotá, Colombia. I recently had meetings about creative for Club Necaxa and the work we're doing with La Equidad. I believe small businesses are what power the world economy. They create the jobs, so anything that helps them access capital, guidance, or infrastructure — I want to be part of that. No matter the project, I write everything down I still write everything down. I love physically writing notes. If I don't write something down, I'll forget it. I'll use my phone notes sometimes, but I prefer paper. I like to physically jot down what I have to do that day. I try to be fully present when I'm with my son At the end of the day, I try really hard to make sure I'm fully present when I'm with my son. On an office day, I try to be out by three to pick up Santi from school. I don't like walking in the door with my phone in my hand. Once I'm home, I play with Santi Then I cook dinner, and we eat at 5 p.m. Next is bath time, books, and bedtime. That time is 100% his. I definitely enjoy a great glass of wine, a fresh baguette, and, of course, tequila. I really believe in balance. I say you should enjoy the things you love. I am, however, militant about my sleep. items.summary_html:
Eva Longoria.

Courtesy of Eva Longoria

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Eva Longoria, a 51-year-old actor, producer, director, and entrepreneur who lives between Spain, Mexico, and the US. It has been edited for length and clarity.

I'm an actor who started in my early 20s. I never imagined it as a career growing up, but after entering a talent contest, I decided to move to LA and give acting a real shot.

My first professional acting jobs were on television. One of my first major TV roles was on "The Young and the Restless." My breakout role came soon after, as Gabrielle Solis on "Desperate Housewives."

Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful leaders in business structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine.

At this point in my career, I'm focused on Hyphenate Media Group, a next-generation media company I cofounded that develops, produces, and invests in culture-defining premium film, television, and digital content.

Here's a day in my life.

I wake up around 5 a.m. with my son, Santi

He's basically my alarm clock. I get up, get dressed, and the first thing I do is make him fresh tortillas every morning.

Then I drink a glass of water before heading to my workout.

I usually work out around 5:30 a.m.

During my hourlong workout, I like to mix it up with heavy strength training and functional movement. I love to bounce and walk. I change my routine pretty often, but consistency is what really matters. It's less about doing the perfect workout and more about showing up every day.

I use amino acids and supplements for training. After that, I have the same breakfast every morning: boiled eggs — no yolk — and turkey sausage.

I eat breakfast in the car with Santi

While I drive him to school, I also drink my water with electrolytes and creatine.

I wear a lot of different hats. My days vary depending on what I'm doing because I'm an entrepreneur at heart, so I'm constantly working on different projects.

I head to the office by 9 a.m.

After dropping Santi off, I'll head to the office. It takes me about an hour. If I have meetings — which I often do — I'll be driven so I can work in the car. Sometimes I take Waymo rides to make it easier.

In the car, I do Zooms, take calls, and answer emails. I also have a lot of Zooms in the morning because I do a lot of work in Europe, and the time difference is hard when I'm in LA.

I try to stack everything early and be very efficient so that once I'm home, I can actually be present.

I take a lot of meetings

When I'm in the office, I'm jumping between meetings about rewrites or reviewing scripts that come in for film development. Every meeting is different.

When the team is all together in the same room, we brainstorm. Sometimes our meetings are development meetings, writer meetings, or pitches. We're in the middle of a lot of pitches right now.

We also have branding meetings constantly — I think we had eight brands come through recently for branded content we're producing.

We have our unscripted side and our scripted side, so I'm meeting with our unscripted executives to go over the slate — who we're selling to, what stage it's at, whether it's sold, pitching, in production, or in post.

When I'm directing, I sometimes shoot 12-hour days

When I'm directing, it feels like full steam ahead. Call time is often 6 a.m., so on those days, I wake up around 4 a.m. to work out at 4:30 a.m. and leave the house by 5:30 a.m. We usually have 12-hour shoots. I don't like running sets that are longer than 12 hours.

On "Desperate Housewives," we would sometimes shoot for 17 or 18 hours. The 18-hour days are gone. People need to go home to their families. You have to have a civilized life. When I shoot in places like Spain or France, there are rules that you can't go above certain hours, and I love that.

When we're shooting, I sometimes stop and realize I haven't eaten all day. My assistant literally has to keep me fed and make sure I'm drinking water.

I go through two big bottles of water a day when I'm on set. Things always feel a bit crazy when I'm directing.

Soccer teams, investments, and building businesses

I also spend time on my other projects — my soccer teams, investments, and entrepreneurial work.

I'm an investor in several soccer clubs, including Angel City FC, Club Necaxa, and La Equidad in Bogotá, Colombia. I recently had meetings about creative for Club Necaxa and the work we're doing with La Equidad.

I believe small businesses are what power the world economy. They create the jobs, so anything that helps them access capital, guidance, or infrastructure — I want to be part of that.

No matter the project, I write everything down

I still write everything down. I love physically writing notes. If I don't write something down, I'll forget it.

I'll use my phone notes sometimes, but I prefer paper. I like to physically jot down what I have to do that day.

I try to be fully present when I'm with my son

At the end of the day, I try really hard to make sure I'm fully present when I'm with my son.

On an office day, I try to be out by three to pick up Santi from school. I don't like walking in the door with my phone in my hand.

Once I'm home, I play with Santi

Then I cook dinner, and we eat at 5 p.m. Next is bath time, books, and bedtime. That time is 100% his.

I definitely enjoy a great glass of wine, a fresh baguette, and, of course, tequila. I really believe in balance. I say you should enjoy the things you love.

I am, however, militant about my sleep.

I'm usually in bed by 8:30 p.m., and I'm out by 9

I always tell people: don't send me an email you need me to look at at night, because I won't see it until the morning.

My weekends are all about family. I love spending time with my son, cooking, working out, getting together with friends, being outdoors, and slowing down whenever I can. If I'm not working, I'm happiest around a table with family, sharing a great meal.

items.title: I dropped out of high school at 16 to become a Buddhist monk. Now I run a startup taking on Accenture.
items.summary: Lilly Chen, founder and CEO of FSH Technologies, just raised $25 million in funding. Outlier Partners 30-year-old Lilly Chen is the founder of FSH Technologies, which recently raised $25 million. FSH Technologies competes with firms like Accenture to help modernize government technology systems. Chen spent two years as a Buddhist monk, which she said taught her valuable leadership lessons. This is a conversation with Lilly Chen, the 30-year-old founder and CEO of FSH Technologies. It has been edited and condensed for clarity. When I was 16, I dropped out of high school and became a Buddhist monk . At the time, I was really sick. I had been diagnosed with Graves' disease, an autoimmune disorder , and my family was on public health insurance. I didn't have good access to preventive healthcare, We went through that cycle two or three times. At one point, I had a fever for more than a week and was bedridden. My mom had always been spiritual. Eventually, she was basically like, "Screw Western medicine. Let's become monks." I got ordained in America, and eventually my mom and I moved to a Buddhist monastery in rural China. I was a monk for about two years altogether, which included about six months living at that monastery. Life there was simple. We woke up at 3 a.m. and meditated. We grew food, cleaned, fetched water, and did other chores. There was no electricity. People also traveled to see the monks, and they would tell us about their problems. They came looking for advice, but monks don't really give advice. We listened. I was a teenager spending every day listening to people talk about their problems. I think that was the most important thing I learned from being a monk: How to listen to other people. I also read constantly. Eventually, the head monk noticed and asked if I liked learning. I told him yes, and that one of the things I missed most about America was having access to public libraries. He said, "I heard that's what university is for." He told me to go back to America, go to college, meet people my own age, and figure out what I found interesting. So I came back to America, but I had no idea how to go to college. I didn't have a high school diploma. I didn't really have anyone helping me navigate the process. My plan was to get a GED , attend community college, and eventually transfer. I went to a college fair at my public library to find my local community college. I saw a table marked "CC" and stopped there, thinking it meant community college. It was actually a small liberal arts school called Colorado College. I told a woman there about my unconventional path. She told me to take the ACT and email her my score. I got a 36, which is the highest possible score. She told me to apply early decision to Colorado College. I asked if I could even do that without a high school diploma. She told me to apply, submit my test score, and write about my experience in my personal essay. She would figure out the rest. I got accepted. In college, I taught myself how to code. After graduating, I became a software engineer at Meta , but I quickly grew tired of it. A year later, I founded FSH Technologies. Lilly Chen, center right, and the FSH Technologies team. Outlier Partners FSH Technologies builds software for cities, school districts, and state agencies, with a focus on replacing slow and outdated government technology systems. We've raised $25 million in total funding, including, most recently, a $20 million Series A led by Lachy Groom, an early investor in companies including Figma, Notion, Ramp, and Lattice. The Series A followed an earlier $5 million seed round led by Contrary and Acrew, with General Catalyst, Scribble, and Basis Set Ventures also participating. The way I think about the company still comes back to something I learned at the monastery. One of my chores there was taking care of a koi pond. The monk who encouraged me to go to college would tell me, "Be the pond, not the fish." His point was that we tend to fixate on one problem — one fish — instead of seeing the whole system. That is how I think about government technology. Software is one fish. There are also procurement rules, existing processes, change management, and people's resistance to change. At FSH, we try to solve the whole problem end-to-end. That also shapes how we compete with consulting firms . We frequently encounter firms like Accenture in government contract bidding, and we have beaten them. Accenture is probably the competitor we see most often. After awards are made, clients will sometimes tell us which other vendors they were considering. One of the biggest differences is our incentives. We don't charge billable consulting hours, and we don't have salespeople or consultants. Everyone at FSH is a builder. I understand why governments still choose established firms like Accenture. The public sector is risk-averse, and there is comfort in hiring a familiar name. My hope is that if we keep delivering successfully, the results will become hard to ignore. items.title: Why Jeff Dean says he left Google after 27 years to build a 4-person AI startup
items.summary: Google's outgoing chief scientist, Jeff Dean. THOMAS SAMSON/AFP via Getty Images Jeff Dean, the former chief scientist at Google, left the company earlier this month after 27 years. Dean is now building his own small AI startup called Discovery Loop. Dean said small startups have key advantages over Big Tech companies. After 27 years, it must have been hard for Jeff Dean to let go. Dean, who quit Google to build his own AI startup called Discovery Loop, briefly choked up while describing his decision to leave the search giant after more than a quarter-century during a talk at Stanford University earlier this month. "They have a plan for making the Gemini models awesome," Dean says in a video of the event released on Tuesday, flashing a thumbs up while appearing to choke back tears. The talk, held on August 7, was his first public appearance since leaving Google. Though Dean built a sterling reputation at Google, leading numerous high-profile projects, he said during the talk that being part of a small startup — four people in Discovery Loop's case — was now not only possible but an optimized vehicle for accelerated innovation. Pointing toward the growing availability of cloud compute, Dean said that smaller startups can now "rely on" Google and other cloud providers to "build out the infrastructure" necessary to power AI work. "That makes it possible for a small set of people to raise a fair bit of capital and be able to use those platforms without having to build them themselves," he said. Working on a smaller team, Dean said, will also allow his startup to cut through "slight distractions" that would ordinarily hamper progress in large organizations. "We're super excited as a small company about working in a really focused way on science and engineering automation," he said. More small companies have been popping up recently as AI agents prove capable of automating processes that once required the work of multiple employees. Modern-day startups are scaling more quickly, and thriving with only a handful of employees. Dean's Discovery Loop, a public benefit company, aims to automate the process by which scientists and engineers propose an experiment, implement and run it, and evaluate the results. Dean said at the talk that he and his cofounders "might make decisions that are not in the company's financial interest but are in the broader societal good." Specifically, Discovery Loop wants to build systems that can tackle parts of the 14 challenges laid out by some of the world's most accomplished scientists and engineers to improve life as we know it. Formerly known as the "National Academy of Engineering Grand Challenges," the 14 topics range from "Reverse Engineer the Brain" to "Prevent Nuclear Terror." A Discovery Loop press release from August 5 said that the company's initial funding round is being led by Radical Ventures and Khosla Ventures, with participation from Lightspeed, Kleiner Perkins, and Doerr Capital. Alphabet is a founding investor and cloud partner, according to Google CEO Sundar Pichai . Business Insider reported last week that Dean has been in talks to raise $1 billion at about a $10 billion valuation. Nevertheless, Dean said creating a new startup still comes with its own anxieties. "It's a little nerve-wracking," he said. "But at the same time it's also exciting." items.title: Inside OpenAI's plan to make ChatGPT the way you use your computer
items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Sebastian Gollnow/picture alliance via Getty Images OpenAI is rolling out its Computer Use tools into ChatGPT, part of a push to automate more work. The tools can perform actions in a computer's apps and work online inside a web browser. OpenAI staff spoke about the technology's capabilities and what still needs to be figured out. OpenAI staffers say they're close to realizing one of the AI lab's longest-standing ambitions. Since the company's 2015 founding, leaders have hoped to one day build AI agents that can use a computer — and, crucially, a web browser — with the same dexterity as a human. A huge challenge has been collecting and creating the data to train these agents. OpenAI now has enough faith in the tech to start rolling out Computer Use tools to customers. This year, the company launched a Chrome extension that lets ChatGPT take over the browser, created cloud and in-app browsers for ChatGPT to interact with public websites, and added Computer Use to its Codex coding tool. The same underlying tech now also lets users have ChatGPT complete tasks on other apps. OpenAI's president, Greg Brockman , wrote on X that an April update made his company's tech "no longer just for coders, but for anyone who does computer work." Employees who work on the tools for OpenAI told Business Insider that while there's room for improvement, the tools are at an inflection point. Rival Anthropic is also racing to improve its version of Computer Use and was the first to market in 2024. As of May, at least 600,000 organizations had tried Anthropic's Claude Cowork feature, which uses the tool. Now, OpenAI says its tech's capabilities have caught up, and it's filling its blockbuster ChatGPT with ways to automate computer tasks, betting that users will turn over more and more work to it. "Once ChatGPT can use computers and software faster than you or I can, it's going to change the way that you, by default, want to interact with your computer," Ari Weinstein, a manager on OpenAI's Computer Use team, told Business Insider. How OpenAI trained and built Computer Use Each phase of training for OpenAI's newest models included data or processes that improved them for Computer Use. Zhou Yu, an AI researcher at Columbia University who worked on a popular benchmark test for computer-use agents, told Business Insider that this type of extra training builds on a standard AI model's capabilities and teaches it how to handle more tasks. At the earliest phase, where OpenAI builds a model's base with a vast amount of data , the company likely included frame-by-frame screenshots, Yu said, to "front-load" helpful information for Computer Use. Then, in a later step, developers can provide the models with data showing the ideal inputs that produce a given output — in this case, the computer functions that lead to that result, such as filling out a tax form or 3D-modeling an object. This data can come from human trainers : OpenAI, when it announced a 2025 version of Computer Use, said it had used datasets where people demonstrated how to complete tasks. (OpenAI declined to provide specifics about its latest training data.) Yu said this type of data is expensive since it's hard to obtain and clean up for use. OpenAI also likely improves the models' computer-use skills by ordering them to try to complete virtual tasks and rewarding successful behavior — known as reinforcement learning, where the model "can learn to do more of these actions that have gotten rewarded," Yu said. OpenAI has upgraded how its models interact with a computer and process data while in use, Weinstein said. Previously, ChatGPT would take a screenshot of a user's computer, analyze pixels, inject a command, and repeat. Now, when the tool has a website open, it can swiftly read the page's guts — its memory structure, accessibility information, and link connections. The tool still takes screenshots; users are asked to let ChatGPT record their screen as they set up Computer Use, so it can rapidly analyze what's on-screen. Weinstein said the mix of tools helps provide OpenAI's Codex with a way to test the code it's built, find bugs, and make improvements in a "full loop." That's the use case for Cristian Medina Ruiz, a hobbyist coder in the Czech Republic. He showed Business Insider his attempt to use Codex to rebuild the 2013 city-building game "SimCity" from its original source code. The Computer Use tool opened a window on his computer to verify that the game correctly simulated car movements and building images. Ruiz said Computer Use got him wholeheartedly into ChatGPT, and he now leaves his code running and iterating when he's away from his computer. "It does these things even when I'm away," he said. OpenAI wants you to use ChatGPT to interact with the open internet Weinstein and James Sun, who works on browser capabilities at OpenAI, told Business Insider that part of the technology's promise is connecting ChatGPT's agents to disparate parts of the internet and its "long tail" of websites. Most online tools are built only for the human hand — an appointment-scheduling website, a company's internal inventory dashboard, a social media platform. Weinstein and Sun said they're seeing users of Computer Use automate data entry work, compliance tasks, and calendar scheduling . Weinstein said that as OpenAI's models have improved over time, they've become better at noticing when things go wrong and correcting them, which helps them finish tasks and avoid going down online rabbit holes. Yu, the Columbia AI researcher, said there's a "gap" between the technology's current speed and the level consumers want. "We definitely do see that computer-use agents could do well in limited domains, when we give it a lot of training data," Yu said. "When you want to generalize to any webpage, any application, any operating system, it's still very difficult." Computer Use can't churn through email responses, and scrolls laggingly through social media feeds. Both Sun and Weinstein hope that as OpenAI's models improve , Computer Use will become so fast that the experience of working online will get the same treatment as coding. "For a lot of engineers now, it's just faster for the agent to code than to code themselves," Sun said. "There's no calculus, you just do it. I think Computer Use will become more and more like that." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman warned of 'potential risks' When OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was discussing an early Computer Use version in 2025, he wrote on X that, "Although the utility is significant, so are the potential risks," and added, "We recommend giving agents the minimum access required to complete a task to reduce privacy and security risks." The fact that OpenAI puts this onus on users worries Mark Beare, a general manager at the security firm Malwarebytes. "This does still feel a little bit wild west-ish to me," Beare told Business Insider, adding that customers might not have enough privacy protections set up and that businesses also struggle to keep pace with AI governance . Beare added that people trying Computer Use should make sure they wall off passwords , sensitive data, and anything under a nondisclosure agreement or protected by privacy law. He said he'd avoid letting an agent run unsupervised on a long, complex task — he worries that a bad actor's website will lure in the bot and try to extract personal information. Sun said his team has been grappling with what he called "confirmation policy," or how often and when the Computer Use tool should ask a user to permit its next step. So far, he said, they've decided that whenever an AI agent transmits data or deletes something, it should ask the user first. Much of doing work online requires quick decisions — Sun said OpenAI is still figuring out the trade-offs of letting AI onto browsers. "You can make something 100% safe, but then it's just very, very difficult to use, and you can make something that is very easy to use but very dangerous," Sun said. "So we're really trying to figure out how to build something that's beneficial and also easy to use." Have a tip? Zhou Yu, an AI researcher at Columbia University who worked on a popular benchmark test for computer-use agents, told Business Insider that this type of extra training builds on a standard AI model's capabilities and teaches it how to handle more tasks.

At the earliest phase, where OpenAI builds a model's base with a vast amount of data, the company likely included frame-by-frame screenshots, Yu said, to "front-load" helpful information for Computer Use.

Then, in a later step, developers can provide the models with data showing the ideal inputs that produce a given output — in this case, the computer functions that lead to that result, such as filling out a tax form or 3D-modeling an object.

This data can come from human trainers: OpenAI, when it announced a 2025 version of Computer Use, said it had used datasets where people demonstrated how to complete tasks. (OpenAI declined to provide specifics about its latest training data.) Yu said this type of data is expensive since it's hard to obtain and clean up for use.

OpenAI also likely improves the models' computer-use skills by ordering them to try to complete virtual tasks and rewarding successful behavior — known as reinforcement learning, where the model "can learn to do more of these actions that have gotten rewarded," Yu said.

OpenAI has upgraded how its models interact with a computer and process data while in use, Weinstein said. Previously, ChatGPT would take a screenshot of a user's computer, analyze pixels, inject a command, and repeat. Now, when the tool has a website open, it can swiftly read the page's guts — its memory structure, accessibility information, and link connections.

The tool still takes screenshots; users are asked to let ChatGPT record their screen as they set up Computer Use, so it can rapidly analyze what's on-screen. Weinstein said the mix of tools helps provide OpenAI's Codex with a way to test the code it's built, find bugs, and make improvements in a "full loop."

That's the use case for Cristian Medina Ruiz, a hobbyist coder in the Czech Republic. He showed Business Insider his attempt to use Codex to rebuild the 2013 city-building game "SimCity" from its original source code. The Computer Use tool opened a window on his computer to verify that the game correctly simulated car movements and building images.

Ruiz said Computer Use got him wholeheartedly into ChatGPT, and he now leaves his code running and iterating when he's away from his computer.

"It does these things even when I'm away," he said.

OpenAI wants you to use ChatGPT to interact with the open internet

Weinstein and James Sun, who works on browser capabilities at OpenAI, told Business Insider that part of the technology's promise is connecting ChatGPT's agents to disparate parts of the internet and its "long tail" of websites.

Most online tools are built only for the human hand — an appointment-scheduling website, a company's internal inventory dashboard, a social media platform. Weinstein and Sun said they're seeing users of Computer Use automate data entry work, compliance tasks, and calendar scheduling.

Weinstein said that as OpenAI's models have improved over time, they've become better at noticing when things go wrong and correcting them, which helps them finish tasks and avoid going down online rabbit holes.

Yu, the Columbia AI researcher, said there's a "gap" between the technology's current speed and the level consumers want.

"We definitely do see that computer-use agents could do well in limited domains, when we give it a lot of training data," Yu said. "When you want to generalize to any webpage, any application, any operating system, it's still very difficult."

Computer Use can't churn through email responses, and scrolls laggingly through social media feeds. Both Sun and Weinstein hope that as OpenAI's models improve, Computer Use will become so fast that the experience of working online will get the same treatment as coding.

"For a lot of engineers now, it's just faster for the agent to code than to code themselves," Sun said. "There's no calculus, you just do it. I think Computer Use will become more and more like that."

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman warned of 'potential risks'

When OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was discussing an early Computer Use version in 2025, he wrote on X that, "Although the utility is significant, so are the potential risks," and added, "We recommend giving agents the minimum access required to complete a task to reduce privacy and security risks."

The fact that OpenAI puts this onus on users worries Mark Beare, a general manager at the security firm Malwarebytes.

"This does still feel a little bit wild west-ish to me," Beare told Business Insider, adding that customers might not have enough privacy protections set up and that businesses also struggle to keep pace with AI governance.

Beare added that people trying Computer Use should make sure they wall off passwords, sensitive data, and anything under a nondisclosure agreement or protected by privacy law. He said he'd avoid letting an agent run unsupervised on a long, complex task — he worries that a bad actor's website will lure in the bot and try to extract personal information.

Sun said his team has been grappling with what he called "confirmation policy," or how often and when the Computer Use tool should ask a user to permit its next step. So far, he said, they've decided that whenever an AI agent transmits data or deletes something, it should ask the user first. Much of doing work online requires quick decisions — Sun said OpenAI is still figuring out the trade-offs of letting AI onto browsers.

"You can make something 100% safe, but then it's just very, very difficult to use, and you can make something that is very easy to use but very dangerous," Sun said. "So we're really trying to figure out how to build something that's beneficial and also easy to use."

items.title: One big thing is dragging down Americans' vibes about the economy
items.summary: Americans' wallets are feeling the strain of inflation outpacing wages. Spencer Platt/Getty Images US consumer sentiment is worse than in the pandemic years. One likely reason is that wage growth isn't keeping up with inflation. The sky-high inflation of a few years ago has had lingering effects on workers. Americans' wages aren't keeping up with the cost of living, and it's likely dragging down how they feel about the economy. The economy is still slowly growing, consumers are still spending, and both unemployment and layoffs are low. However, consumer sentiment, as measured by the University of Michigan's monthly survey, remains worse than during the COVID period. One big factor could explain why: Inflation has exceeded wage growth for four straight months. "Consumers' frustration over the erosion of their purchasing power continues to mount," Joanne Hsu, University of Michigan's surveys of consumers director, said. The survey showed almost three-quarters of consumers in August thought price growth would outpace their income growth over the next year. Hsu said many people are worried that higher energy prices will affect other parts of the economy. "A sustained drop in gasoline prices over the course of several months (in contrast to temporary dips) would go a long way in boosting consumer views of the economy," Hsu said. Wage growth lagging inflation is not the only concerning trend in the economy. For instance, labor force participation is at its lowest level in decades outside the pandemic. However, it can be tough for consumers to ignore the higher prices blasted on gas station signs and posted along grocery aisles. How has your financial circumstance changed over the past year? Have you dipped into savings, got a raise that didn't keep up with inflation, or had to cut back on certain expenses? Reach out to this reporter to share at mhoff@businessinsider.com . Even though inflation is down from its post-COVID peak, it's still above historical norms, and the long-running impact of that spike is still being felt in Americans' wallets years later. A new working paper from The University of Chicago Booth School of Business's Erik Hurst and Christina Patterson, and ADP Research's Nela Richardson and Liv Wang, used ADP's payroll data through 2025 to examine purchasing power . They found that the unexpected and temporary inflation shock as the economy reopened in the wake of the pandemic resulted in a "persistent downward shift in real wages, helping explain why Americans' dissatisfaction outlasted the inflation episode itself." The researchers found that real wages fell between December 2020 and 2024 for nearly 40% of workers, higher than the roughly 24% of workers pre-pandemic. " Inflation has slowed , but many people never fully recovered the purchasing power they lost when prices surged," Richardson said in a blog post about the findings. She said that a 3% raise was usually sufficient to get a "modest" real income gain pre-pandemic. She added that when inflation skyrocketed in 2022, employers gave raises that didn't keep pace with the higher inflation. "Hence this once-in-a-generation inflation shock led to a decline in U.S. consumer purchasing power that persists today," she said. Despite an uptick in the average share of workers getting a bonus from 2021 to 2023 compared to 2017 to 2019, the researchers found bonuses "did very little to stem the real wage losses that workers experienced." Off-cycle raises helped moderate real wage declines for job stayers. The importance of real wage gains Mark Hamrick, chief economic analyst at The Hamrick Brief, told Business Insider that persistently high inflation above the Fed's 2% target is contributing to Americans' pessimistic feelings about the economy. "Americans are literally paying the price for high inflation through elevated price levels," he said. "Even if you're making more money numbers-wise, with the way prices are rising, you have less money left over at the end of the month," ZipRecruiter economist Nicole Bachaud told Business Insider. "That's really going to impact the large consumer base of America, middle- and low-income households, who are really dependent on wage growth to help them remain economically viable." People with different levels of wealth aren't experiencing the economy equally . Hamrick said those lacking substantial wealth are constantly reminded of the gap. As an example, he noted that on many airlines, higher-paying passengers at the front of the plane typically receive a higher level of service than "those who sit in the back and are scrunched up." "At the end of the day, it's affordability challenges and a growing wealth divide that ends up disenfranchising a good number of people," he said. While Hamrick said there will always be divides in wealth, sustained wage gains adjusted for inflation would help mitigate the problem, which hasn't been happening in aggregate. "A number of people are being taken financial prisoner by that," he said. Reach out to this reporter to share how the economy has affected you financially, at mhoff@businessinsider.com .
